title: Damping-Off Biology and Prevention
objective: Recognize pre- and post-emergence damping-off risk and build prevention around sanitation, drainage, environment, and early removal.

terms.definition: Disease syndrome in which seed or young seedlings rot before emergence or collapse soon after emergence.
Fungus-like organism; several Pythium or related taxa cause seed and root disease.
Pathogen propagules capable of initiating infection.
Interaction of a susceptible host, a capable pathogen, and a favorable environment.

coreScience: Damping-off is a syndrome, not one organism. Cannabis and general seedling literature identify Pythium or related oomycetes, Fusarium species, Rhizoctonia solani, and other organisms as potential causes. Pre-emergence disease appears as seed decay or missing seedlings. Post-emergence disease can produce water-soaked or constricted stem tissue, root discoloration, wilting, lodging, and collapse.

Young seedlings are vulnerable because tissues are tender and reserves are limited. Wet, poorly drained, compacted, contaminated, or slow-growing conditions can favor disease. Temperature effects depend on the pathogen and host; 'cold and wet' is a common risk pattern but not a complete rule for every organism.

Prevention uses multiple barriers: traceable vigorous seed, clean trays and tools, appropriate new or treated medium, clean water practices, drainage, noncompacted media, controlled humidity, air movement, prompt emergence, spacing, scouting, and removal of diseased material. A pesticide or biological product is not automatically legal or effective on cannabis; the current label and jurisdiction control its use.

Disease development requires convergence of susceptible tissue, viable inoculum, and a favorable environment. Excess moisture can increase infection opportunity by slowing host growth, reducing root-zone aeration, and moving propagules through splash or shared water, but wetness alone is not the pathogen. Conversely, clean-looking media can still contain inoculum. Distribution patterns—such as clustering by tray, water path, seed lot, bench, or reused container—are therefore valuable epidemiological evidence when combined with lesion morphology and testing.
cultivationRelevance: Quarantine affected trays, stop shared drainage or splash pathways, remove diseased units without contacting healthy seedlings, and clean hands, tools, benches, and containers according to the sanitation plan.
Do not diagnose by collapse alone. Document stem and root lesions, environmental history, distribution pattern, and laboratory results when consequences justify testing.

Treat the first collapsing seedling as a biosecurity event rather than simply increasing airflow. Isolate the affected tray or irrigation path, stop movement of shared runoff, inspect neighboring units, remove symptomatic material carefully, and sanitize hands/tools/benches according to the controlled sanitation procedure.

Use comparisons to distinguish environment from infectious spread. Map which cells and trays are affected, compare moisture/drainage and temperature, review media/seed/water/tool sources, and submit representative symptomatic tissue for laboratory identification when the consequence justifies it. Preserve untreated evidence before applying any authorized control.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record affected and total seedlings by tray, lot, cell/position, bench, date, and developmental stage. Recount at defined intervals so spread rate and clustering can be evaluated.
Record pre-emergence loss, hypocotyl constriction, water-soaked tissue, root discoloration, lesions, collapse, decay, odor, and photographs with scale. Distinguish root, crown, and stem locations.
Record media moisture/dryback, drainage/standing water, substrate batch/packing, temperature, humidity, airflow, light, irrigation method, and root-zone salinity/pH history where relevant.
Trace seed lot, media batch, reused tray, bench, water source, irrigation line, shared runoff, tools, hands, insects, propagation area, and movement of plants or equipment.
Record microscopy/culture/molecular or other laboratory findings when obtained, sample ID and collection site, plus which causal organisms remain plausible if no test was performed.
Record isolation, removal, sanitation method, environmental correction, legally authorized treatment if any, operator/date, subsequent incidence, and whether new cases stop or continue.

misconceptions: Damping-off is always one fungus: Multiple fungi and oomycetes can cause the syndrome.
Cinnamon proves or cures the diagnosis: Anecdotal household treatments do not identify the pathogen or replace prevention.
More airflow alone solves it: Disease control also depends on sanitation, moisture, drainage, seed vigor, and pathogen pressure.
evidenceLimits: Damping-off is a syndrome caused by multiple fungi and oomycetes, and visual collapse or stem constriction rarely establishes the causal organism to species. Environmental conditions influence host susceptibility and pathogen activity differently by organism. Laboratory detection also requires representative sampling and interpretation. Any pesticide, disinfectant, biological, or other regulated product must be legal for the crop, site, and jurisdiction and used according to the current label; this lesson does not prescribe a pesticide.
